message_2_subject: Re: Quick follow-up: model fit + streaming UX (post-call)
message_2_body:
Marissa — thanks for the recap. A couple clarifying Qs so we prep the right sample set:

1) For the streaming evals, can you confirm whether the partial outputs we'll see during token streaming will include punctuation-complete sentences or might cut mid-sentence? We need to ensure the UI doesn't display garbled fragments to clinicians.
2) Stop-sequence behavior: our notes often have templates and embedded tags (e.g., [SIGNOFF]). Can Jordan's team support configurable stop tokens and early flush?
3) For latency SLOs, our target is 95% of tokens under 150ms during normal load, and 99th under 350ms. Is that realistic on Dedicated or Hosted?

message_3_subject: Re: Quick follow-up: model fit + streaming UX (post-call)
message_3_body:
Hi Tom — great questions, answered inline below. Forwarding a short streaming playbook (attached) with examples and a recommended prompt-set.

1) Partial outputs & mid-sentence cuts:
- Token streaming by design streams as tokens are generated; partial outputs can cut mid-sentence. UX best practice is to treat streaming as "progressive render" and show a visual indicator until the model emits a final stop token or the server sends a "done" frame. We recommend buffering at the UI for short windows (50-100ms) and only committing lines once punctuation or a stop token appears. This reduces perceived garble.

2) Stop-sequence handling:
- Redwood supports configurable stop sequences per request. For embedded templates like [SIGNOFF], include that as a stop token in the prompt or in the request stop list. We also support suffix-based post-processing to strip trailing fragments.

3) Latency SLOs (95% <150ms, 99% <350ms):
- Hosted: achievable for smaller models (13B quantized) with proper batching and autoscaling; 70B will typically target higher latency unless on Dedicated with GPU pools tuned for that model.
- Dedicated: recommended if you need consistent 99th percentile latency at high concurrency — we can size a Dedicated pool to hit the SLOs but we'll need expected RPS and sequence-length distribution.

Recommended models for your evals:
- redwood-rlm-13b-q4: cost-efficient, good streaming behavior, 13B family for standard clinical summarization.
- redwood-rlm-70b-fp16: highest-quality for clinical nuance; expect higher latency and cost.

Prompt-set recommendations (short example):
- System: "You are an assistant that converts clinician encounter notes into a concise structured summary. Do not hallucinate facts; mark uncertain items as "[UNCERTAIN]"."
- Example user prompt 1: "Summarize the following encounter in 5 bullet points and flag medication changes: <CLINICAL_TEXT>"
- Stop tokens: ["\n\n", "[SIGNOFF]", ""])

I've attached redwood-streaming-playbook.pdf and a sample prompt-set in the Drive folder: https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1a2b3c-acme-evals.

If you send the sample prompts by Tue (3/17), we can run a 1-2 day eval and share model outputs + qualitative regression notes. If you prefer, we can also schedule a 30-min demo with live streaming to show UX considerations.

Jordan
Jordan Blake
Solutions Engineer | Redwood Inference
